newsitem.title: INDIA: India's HFCL sees jump in 96/97 profits.
newsitem.headline: India's HFCL sees jump in 96/97 profits.

text.p: Indian telecommunications firm Himachal Futuristic Communications Ltd (HFCL) said on Thursday it expects turnover and net profit to jump 20-30 percent in 1996/97 (April-March) despite a political controversy.

The little known company from the northern state of Himachal Pradesh captured public attention last year when it offered a staggering $27 billion for licences to set up basic telephone services in nine of India's 21 telephone zones.
Opposition parties, alleging that former communications minister Sukh Ram had favoured HFCL in the tendering process, paralysed parliament for nearly a month in late 1995 in protest.
Both HFCL and Sukh Ram, a senior leader from Himachal Pradesh currently under arrest in a corruption case, have denied the accusation.
"The only thing which is common between HFCL and the minister is the word Himachal," HFCL executive director Arvind Kharbanda told Reuters in an interview.
Asked if the controversy would affect the company's performance in 1996/97, Kharbanda said: "We expect a normal 20 to 30 percent growth in net profit and turnover."

HFCL, which currently makes telecommunications equipment and offers services like satellite communications and radio paging, posted turnover of 2.6 billion rupees ($72.8 million) in 1995/96 and net profit of 400 million rupees, he said.
HFCL is the leading partner in HFCL-Bezeq Telecom Ltd, a consortium which includes Israel's Bezeq Telecom and Thailand's Shinawatra group.
The consortium has won four licences, including one for lucrative Delhi. A fourth round of bidding is yet to be held.
The licences have not yet been awarded because of disputes between the state-run telephone company and the private firms which are set to end the government's telecommunications monopoly.

Federal police have accused Sukh Ram of receiving kickbacks and amassing wealth beyond his means. He was arrested on Monday at New Delhi's international airport as he returned to India from London. No charges have been filed.
Kharbanda said the political controversy had slowed down the privatisation process. "The whole process of privatisation has suffered," he said.

Kharbanda said HFCL's fortunes would be partially affected by the controversy as the government's Department of Telecommunications (DOT) had decided to review many of the tenders it awarded in the past two years.
"Because of this process in the DOT, there are cancellations of a lot of tenders," he said. "Some of our tenders are also hanging in the process".
But he said HFCL would stand to gain from other tenders not run by DOT.
